{{Short description|Concept within complex analysis}}
{{redirect|Hardy class|the warships|Hardy class destroyer}}
In [[complex analysis]], the '''Hardy spaces''' (or '''Hardy classes''') <math>H^p</math> are [[Function_space|spaces]] of [[holomorphic function]]s on the [[unit disk]] or [[upper half plane]]. They were introduced by [[Frigyes Riesz]] {{harv|Riesz|1923}}, who named them after [[G. H. Hardy]], because of the paper {{harv|Hardy|1915}}. In [[real analysis]] '''Hardy spaces''' are spaces of [[Distribution (mathematics)|distributions]] on the real {{mvar|n}}-space <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>, defined (in the sense of distributions) as boundary values of the holomorphic functions. Hardy spaces are related to the [[Lp space|''L<sup>p</sup>'' spaces]].{{sfn|Folland|2001}} For <math>1 \leq p < \infty</math> these Hardy spaces are [[subset]]s of [[Lp space|<math>L^p</math> spaces]], while for <math>0<p<1</math> the <math>L^p</math> spaces have some undesirable properties, and the Hardy spaces are much better behaved. Hence, <math>H^p</math> spaces can be considered extensions of <math>L^p</math> spaces.{{sfn|Stein|Murphy|1993|p=88}}

Hardy spaces have a number of applications, both in [[mathematical analysis]] itself as well as in interdisciplinary areas such as [[control theory]] (e.g. [[H infinity|<math>H^{\infty}</math> methods]]) and [[scattering theory]].

== Definition ==
===On the unit disk===
The Hardy space <math>H^p</math> for <math>0 < p < \infty</math> is the class of [[holomorphic functions]] <math>f</math> on the open [[unit disk]] <math> \mathbb{D} = \{ z\in \mathbb{C} : |z|<1\} </math> satisfying
<math display="block">\sup_{0\,\leqslant\, r\,<\,1}\left(\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi}\left|f \left (re^{i\theta}\right )\right|^p \; \mathrm{d}\theta\right)^\frac{1}{p}<\infty.</math>
If <math>p \geq 1</math>, this coincides with the definition of the Hardy space <math>p</math>-norm, denoted by <math>\|f\|_{H^p}.</math>

The space <math>H^\infty</math> is defined as the vector space of bounded holomorphic functions on the unit disk, with norm

:<math>{\|f\|}_{H^\infty} = \sup_{|z|< 1} \left|f(z)\right|.</math>

For <math>0<p\leq q\leq\infty</math>, the class <math>H^q</math> is  a [[subset]] of <math>H^p</math>, and the <math>H^p</math>-norm is increasing with <math>p</math> (it is a consequence of [[Hölder's inequality]] that the <math>L^p</math>-norm is increasing for [[Probability space|probability measures]], i.e. [[Measure (mathematics)|measures]] with total mass 1) {{harv|Rudin|1987|loc=Def 17.7}}.

<math>H^2</math> is a [[Hilbert space]], and it is unitarily equivalent to <math>\ell^2(\N)</math> via the unitary map <math>\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^n \leftrightarrow (a_n)_{n=0}^\infty</math>.<ref name="GMR2023">{{Harvard citation|Garcia|Mashreghi|Ross|2023|loc=Sec. 5.3}}</ref>

===On the unit circle===
The Hardy spaces can also be viewed as closed vector subspaces of the complex [[Lp space|''L<sup>p</sup>'' spaces]] on the [[unit circle]] <math>\mathbb T = \{ z \in \C : |z| = 1 \}</math>. This connection is provided by the following theorem {{harv|Katznelson|1976|loc=Thm 3.8}}:  Given <math>f \in H^{p}</math> with <math>p\geq 1</math>, the radial limit
<math display="block">\tilde f\!\left(e^{i\theta}\right) = \lim_{r\to 1} \,f\!\left(re^{i\theta}\right)</math>
exists for almost every <math>\theta</math> and <math>\tilde f \in L^{p}(\mathbb{T})</math> such that {{clarify|reason=Also when p is less than 1?|date=February 2017}}
<math display="block">{\|\tilde f\|}_{L^p} = {\|f\|}_{H^p}.</math>
Denote by <math>H^{p}(\mathbb{T})</math> the vector subspace of <math>L^{p}(\mathbb{T})</math> consisting of all limit functions <math>\tilde f</math>, when <math>f</math> varies in <math>H^{p}</math>, one then has that for ''p''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;1,{{harv|Katznelson|1976}}

:<math>g\in H^p\left(\mathbb{T}\right)\text{ if and only if } g\in L^p\left(\mathbb{T}\right)\text{ and } \hat{g}_{n} =0 \text{ for all } n < 0,</math>
where the <math>\hat{g}_{n}</math> are the [[Fourier coefficients]] defined as
<math display="block">\hat{g}_{n} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} g\left(e^{i\phi}\right) e^{-in\phi} \, \mathrm{d}\phi, \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}.</math>
The space <math>H^{p}(\mathbb{T})</math> is a closed subspace of <math>L^{p}(\mathbb{T})</math>. Since <math>L^{p}(\mathbb{T})</math> is a [[Banach space]] (for <math>1\leq p\leq \infty</math>), so is <math>H^{p}(\mathbb{T})</math>.

The above can be turned around.  Given a function <math>\tilde f \in L^p (\mathbf T)</math>, with ''p'' ≥ 1, one can regain a ([[Harmonic function|harmonic]]) function ''f'' on the unit disk by means of the [[Poisson kernel]] ''P<sub>r</sub>'':

:<math>f\left(re^{i\theta}\right)=\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} P_r(\theta-\phi) \tilde f\left(e^{i\phi}\right) \,\mathrm{d}\phi, \quad r < 1,</math>

and ''f'' belongs to ''H<sup>p</sup>'' exactly when <math>\tilde f</math> is in ''H<sup>p</sup>''('''T'''). Supposing that <math>\tilde f</math> is in ''H<sup>p</sup>''('''T'''), i.e., <math>\tilde f</math> has Fourier coefficients (''a<sub>n</sub>'')<sub>''n''∈'''Z'''</sub> with ''a<sub>n</sub>'' = 0 for every ''n'' < 0, then the associated holomorphic function ''f'' of ''H<sup>p</sup>'' is given by
<math display="block">f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^n, \ \ \ |z| < 1.</math>
In applications, those functions with vanishing negative Fourier coefficients are commonly interpreted as the [[Causal_system|causal]] solutions. For example, the [[H square| Hardy space {{math|''H''<sup>2</sup>}}]] consists of functions whose [[root mean square|mean square value]] remains bounded as <math>r \to 1</math> from below.
Thus, the space ''H''<sup>2</sup> is seen to sit naturally inside [[Square-integrable_function|{{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>}} space]], and is represented by [[infinite sequence]]s indexed by '''N'''; whereas ''L''<sup>2</sup> consists of [[bi-infinite sequence]]s indexed by '''Z'''.

===On the upper half plane===
The Hardy space on the [[upper half-plane]] <math>\mathbb{H} = \{x + iy \mid y > 0;\ x, y \in \mathbb{R} \} </math> is defined to be the space of holomorphic functions <math>f</math> on <math>\mathbb{H}</math> with bounded norm, given by
<math display="block">\|f\|_{H^p} = \sup_{y>0} \left ( \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}|f(x+ iy)|^p\, \mathrm{d}x \right)^{\frac{1}{p}}.</math>
The corresponding <math>H^{\infty}(\mathbb{H})</math> is defined as functions of bounded norm, with the norm given by
<math display="block">\|f\|_{H^\infty} = \sup_{z\in\mathbb{H}}|f(z)|.</math>
The unit disk is [[isomorphic]] to the upper half-plane by means of a [[Möbius transformation]]. For example, let <math>m: \mathbb{D}\rightarrow \mathbb{H}</math> denote the Möbius transformation
<math display="block">m(z)= i \frac{1+z}{1-z}.</math>
Then the linear operator <math>M:H^2(\mathbb{H}) \rightarrow H^2(\mathbb{D})</math> defined by
<math display="block">(Mf)(z):=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{1-z} f(m(z)),</math>
is an [[isometry|isometric]] [[isomorphism]] of Hardy spaces.

A similar approach applies to, e.g., the right half-plane.

=== On the real vector space===
In analysis on the real vector space <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>, the Hardy space <math>H^p</math> (for <math>0 < p \leq \infty</math>) consists of [[Distribution (mathematics)#Tempered distributions and Fourier transform|tempered distributions]] <math>f</math> such that for some [[Schwartz function]] <math>\Phi</math> with <math>\int\Phi = 1</math>, the [[maximal function]]

:<math>(M_\Phi f)(x)=\sup_{t>0}|(f*\Phi_t)(x)|</math>

is in <math>L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)</math>, where <math>*</math> is convolution and <math>\Phi_t(x) = t^{-n}\Phi(x/t)</math>. The <math>H^p</math>-[[quasinorm]] <math>\|f\|_{H^p}</math> of a distribution <math>f</math> of <math>H^p</math> is defined to be the <math>L^p</math> norm of <math>M_\Phi f</math> (this depends on the choice of <math>\Phi</math>, but different choices of Schwartz functions <math>\Phi</math> give equivalent norms).  The <math>H^p</math>-quasinorm is a norm when <math>p \geq 1</math>, but not when <math>p < 1 </math>.

If <math>1 < p < \infty</math>, the Hardy space <math>H^p</math> is the same vector space as <math>L^p</math>, with equivalent norm. When <math>p=1</math>, the Hardy space <math>H^1</math>  is a proper subspace of <math>L^1</math>.  One can find sequences in <math>H^1</math>  that are bounded in <math>L^1</math> but unbounded in <math>H^1</math>; for example, on the line

:<math> f_k(x) = \mathbf{1}_{[0, 1]}(x - k) -  \mathbf{1}_{[0, 1]}(x + k), \ \ \ k > 0.</math>

The <math>L^1</math> and <math>H^1</math> norms are not equivalent on <math>H^1</math>, and <math>H^1</math> is not closed in <math>L^1</math>.  The dual of <math>H^1</math> is the space <math>\operatorname{BMO}</math> of functions of [[bounded mean oscillation]].  The space <math>\operatorname{BMO}</math> contains unbounded functions (proving again that <math>H^1</math> is not closed in <math>L^1</math>).

If <math>p<1</math> then the Hardy space <math>H^p</math> has elements that are not functions, and its dual is the homogeneous Lipschitz space of order <math> n(1/p-1)</math>. When '<math>p < 1</math>, the <math>H^p</math>-quasinorm is not  a norm, as it is not subadditive. The <math>p</math>-th power <math>\|f\|^p_{H^p}</math> is subadditive for <math>p<1</math> and so defines a metric on the Hardy space <math>H^p</math>, which defines the topology and makes <math>H^p</math> into a complete metric space.

==== Atomic decomposition ====
When <math>0 < p \leq 1</math>, a bounded measurable function <math>f</math> of compact support is in the Hardy space <math>H^p</math> if and only if all its moments

:<math>\int_{\mathbf{R}^n} f(x)x_1^{i_1}\ldots x_n^{i_n}\, \mathrm{d}x, </math>

whose order <math>i_1+\cdots+i_n</math> is at most <math>n(1/p-1)</math>, vanish. For example, the integral of <math>f</math> must vanish in order that <math>f \in H^p</math>, <math>0 < p \leq 1</math>, and as long as <math>p > n/(n+1)</math>, this is also sufficient.

If in addition <math>f</math> has support in some ball <math>B</math> and is bounded by <math>|B|^{-1/p}</math>, then <math>f</math> is called an '''<math>H^p</math>-atom''' (here <math>|B|</math> denotes the Euclidean volume of <math>B</math> in <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>).  The <math>H^p</math>-quasinorm of an arbitrary <math>H^p</math>-atom is bounded by a constant depending only on <math>p</math> and on the Schwartz function <math>\Phi</math>.

When <math>0 < p \leq 1</math>, any element <math>f</math> of <math>H^p</math> has an '''atomic decomposition''' as a convergent infinite combination of <math>H^p</math>-atoms,

:<math>f = \sum c_j a_j, \ \ \ \sum |c_j|^p < \infty</math>

where the <math>a_j</math> are <math>H^p</math>-atoms and the <math>c_j</math> are scalars.

On the line, for example, the difference of Dirac distributions <math>f = \delta_1 - \delta_0</math> can be represented as a series of [[Haar wavelet|Haar functions]], convergent in <math>H^p</math>-quasinorm when <math> 1/2 < p < 1 </math>. (On the circle, the corresponding representation is valid for <math> 0 < p < 1 </math>, but on the line, Haar functions do not belong to <math>H^p</math> when <math> p \leq 1/2 </math>, because their maximal function is equivalent at infinity to <math>ax^{-2}</math> for some <math> a \neq 0</math>.)

== Link between real- and complex-variable Hardy spaces ==
Real-variable techniques, mainly associated to the study of ''real Hardy spaces'' defined on '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>, are also used in the simpler framework of the circle. It is a common practice to allow for complex functions (or distributions) in these "real" spaces.  The definition that follows does not distinguish between real or complex case.

Let ''P<sub>r</sub>'' denote the Poisson kernel on the unit circle '''T'''. For a distribution ''f'' on the unit circle, set

:<math>(M f)(e^{i\theta})=\sup_{0<r<1} \left |(f * P_r) \left(e^{i\theta} \right)\right|,</math>

where the ''star'' indicates convolution between the distribution ''f'' and the function e<sup>iθ</sup> → ''P<sub>r</sub>''(θ) on the circle.  Namely, (''f'' ∗ ''P<sub>r</sub>'')(e<sup>iθ</sup>) is the result of the action of ''f'' on the ''C''<sup>∞</sup>-function defined on the unit circle by

:<math>e^{i\varphi} \rightarrow P_r(\theta - \varphi).</math>

For 0&nbsp;< ''p''&nbsp;< ∞, the ''real Hardy space'' ''H<sup>p</sup>''('''T''') consists of distributions ''f'' such that ''M&nbsp;f''&thinsp; is in ''L<sup>p</sup>''('''T''').

The function ''F'' defined on the unit disk by ''F''(''re''<sup>iθ</sup>) = (''f'' ∗ ''P<sub>r</sub>'')(e<sup>iθ</sup>) is harmonic, and ''M&nbsp;f''&thinsp; is the ''radial maximal function'' of ''F''. When ''M&nbsp;f''&thinsp; belongs to ''L<sup>p</sup>''('''T''') and ''p''&nbsp;&ge;&nbsp;1, the distribution ''f''&thinsp; "''is''" a function in ''L<sup>p</sup>''('''T'''), namely the boundary value of ''F''. For ''p''&nbsp;&ge; 1, the ''real Hardy space'' ''H<sup>p</sup>''('''T''') is a subset of ''L<sup>p</sup>''('''T''').

=== Conjugate function ===
To every real trigonometric polynomial ''u'' on the unit circle, one associates the real ''conjugate polynomial'' ''v'' such that ''u'' + i''v'' extends to a holomorphic function in the unit disk,

:<math> u(e^{i\theta}) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{k \geqslant 1} a_k \cos(k \theta) + b_k \sin(k \theta) \longrightarrow v(e^{i\theta}) = \sum_{k \geqslant 1} a_k \sin(k \theta) - b_k \cos(k \theta). </math>

This mapping ''u'' → ''v'' extends to a bounded linear operator ''H'' on ''L<sup>p</sup>''('''T'''), when 1&nbsp;< ''p''&nbsp;< ∞ (up to a scalar multiple, it is the [[Hilbert transform]] on the unit circle), and ''H'' also maps ''L''<sup>1</sup>('''T''') to [[Lp space#Weak Lp|weak-''L''<sup>1</sup>('''T''')]]. When 1&nbsp;&le; ''p''&nbsp;< ∞, the following are equivalent for a ''real valued'' integrable function ''f'' on the unit circle:
* the function ''f'' is the real part of some function ''g'' ∈ ''H<sup>p</sup>''('''T''')
* the function ''f'' and its conjugate ''H(f)'' belong to ''L<sup>p</sup>''('''T''')
* the radial maximal function ''M f''&thinsp;  belongs to ''L<sup>p</sup>''('''T''').

When 1 < ''p'' < ∞, ''H(f)'' belongs to ''L<sup>p</sup>''('''T''') when ''f'' ∈ ''L<sup>p</sup>''('''T'''), hence the real Hardy space ''H<sup>p</sup>''('''T''') coincides with ''L<sup>p</sup>''('''T''') in this case. For ''p'' = 1,  the real Hardy space ''H''<sup>1</sup>('''T''') is a proper subspace of ''L''<sup>1</sup>('''T''').

The case of ''p'' = ∞ was excluded from the definition of real Hardy spaces, because the maximal function ''M&nbsp;f''&thinsp; of an ''L''<sup>∞</sup> function is always bounded, and because it is not desirable that real-''H''<sup>∞</sup> be equal to ''L''<sup>∞</sup>. However, the two following properties are equivalent for a real valued function ''f''
* the function ''f''&thinsp; is the real part of some function ''g'' ∈ ''H''<sup>∞</sup>('''T''')
* the function ''f''&thinsp; and its conjugate ''H(f)'' belong to ''L''<sup>∞</sup>('''T''').

=== For 0 < ''p'' < 1 ===
When 0 < ''p'' < 1, a function ''F'' in ''H<sup>p</sup>'' cannot be reconstructed from the real part of its boundary limit ''function'' on the circle, because of the lack of convexity of ''L<sup>p</sup>'' in this case.  Convexity fails but a kind of "''complex convexity''" remains, namely the fact that ''z'' → |''z''|<sup>''q''</sup> is [[Subharmonic function#Subharmonic functions in the complex plane|subharmonic]] for every ''q'' > 0. As a consequence, if

:<math> F(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} c_n z^n, \quad |z| < 1</math>

is in ''H<sup>p</sup>'', it can be shown that ''c<sub>n</sub>'' = O(''n''<sup>1/''p''–1</sup>). It follows that the Fourier series

:<math> \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} c_n e^{in \theta}</math>

converges in the sense of distributions to a distribution ''f'' on the unit circle, and ''F''(''re''<sup>iθ</sup>)&nbsp;=(''f''&nbsp;∗&nbsp;''P<sub>r</sub>'')(θ).  The function ''F'' ∈ ''H<sup>p</sup>'' can be reconstructed from the real distribution Re(''f'') on the circle, because the Taylor coefficients ''c<sub>n</sub>'' of ''F'' can be computed from the Fourier coefficients of Re(''f'').

Distributions on the circle are general enough for handling Hardy spaces when ''p''&nbsp;<&nbsp;1. Distributions that are not functions do occur, as is seen with functions ''F''(''z'') = (1−''z'')<sup>−''N''</sup> (for |''z''| < 1), that belong to ''H<sup>p</sup>'' when 0&nbsp;< ''N''&nbsp;''p''&nbsp;< 1 (and ''N'' an integer ≥&nbsp;1).

A real distribution on the circle belongs to real-''H<sup>p</sup>''('''T''') iff it is the boundary value of the real part of some ''F'' ∈ ''H<sup>p</sup>''. A Dirac distribution δ<sub>''x''</sub>, at any point ''x'' of the unit circle, belongs to real-''H<sup>p</sup>''('''T''') for every ''p'' < 1; derivatives δ′<sub>''x''</sub> belong when ''p'' < 1/2, second derivatives δ′′<sub>''x''</sub> when ''p'' < 1/3, and so on.

== Beurling factorization ==
For 0&nbsp;<&nbsp;''p''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;∞, every non-zero function ''f'' in ''H<sup>p</sup>'' can be written as the product ''f'' = ''Gh'' where ''G'' is an ''outer function'' and ''h'' is an ''inner function'', as defined below {{harv|Rudin|1987|loc=Thm 17.17}}. This "[[Arne Beurling|Beurling]] factorization" allows the Hardy space to be completely characterized by the spaces of inner and outer functions.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Beurling, Arne|title=On two problems concerning linear transformations in Hilbert space|journal= [[Acta Mathematica]] |volume=81|year=1948|pages=239–255|doi=10.1007/BF02395019|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Inner and outer functions on Riemann surfaces|author=Voichick, Michael|author2=Zalcman, Lawrence|author-link2=Lawrence Zalcman|journal= [[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=16|issue=6|year=1965 |pages=1200–1204|doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1965-0183883-1|doi-access=free}}</ref>

One says that ''G''(''z''){{clarify|rason=What is the doamin?|date=February 2017}} is an '''outer (exterior) function''' if it takes the form

:<math>G(z) = c\, \exp\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{e^{i\theta}+z}{e^{i\theta}-z} \log\!\left(\varphi\!\left(e^{i\theta} \right)\right)\, \mathrm{d}\theta \right)</math>

for some complex number ''c'' with |''c''| = 1, and some positive measurable function <math>\varphi </math> on the unit circle such that <math>\log(\varphi) </math> is integrable on the circle.  In particular, when <math>\varphi </math> is integrable on the circle, ''G'' is in ''H''<sup>1</sup> because the above takes the form of the [[Poisson kernel]] {{harv|Rudin|1987|loc=Thm 17.16}}.  This implies that

:<math>\lim_{r\to 1^-}\left|G\left (re^{i\theta} \right)\right| = \varphi \left(e^{i\theta}\right )</math>

for almost every θ.

One says that ''h'' is an '''inner (interior) function''' if and only if |''h''|&nbsp;≤&nbsp;1 on the unit disk and the limit

:<math>\lim_{r\to 1^-} h(re^{i\theta})</math>

exists for [[almost all]] θ and its [[Absolute value|modulus]] is equal to 1 a.e.  In particular, ''h'' is in ''H''<sup>∞</sup>.{{clarify|reason=Is the converse also true?|date=February 2017}} The inner function can be further factored into a form involving a [[Blaschke product]].

The function ''f'', decomposed as ''f'' = ''Gh'',{{clarify|reason=Very confusing. What class of functions is f drawn from? Is the decomposition supposed to exist or be unique?|date=February 2017}} is in ''H<sup>p</sup>'' if and only if φ belongs to ''L<sup>p</sup>''('''T'''), where φ is the positive function in the representation of the outer function ''G''.

Let ''G'' be an outer function represented as above from a function φ on the circle. Replacing φ by φ<sup>α</sup>, α > 0, a family (''G''<sub>α</sub>) of outer functions is obtained, with the properties:

:''G''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;= ''G'', ''G''<sub>α+β</sub> = ''G''<sub>α</sub>&nbsp;''G''<sub>β</sub>&nbsp; and |''G''<sub>α</sub>| = |''G''|<sup>α</sup> almost everywhere on the circle.

It follows that whenever 0 < ''p'', ''q'', ''r'' < ∞ and 1/''r'' = 1/''p'' + 1/''q'', every function ''f'' in ''H<sup>r</sup>'' can be expressed as the product of a function in ''H<sup>p</sup>'' and a function in ''H<sup>q</sup>''. For example: every function in ''H''<sup>1</sup> is the product of two functions in ''H''<sup>2</sup>; every function in ''H<sup>p</sup>'', ''p'' < 1, can be expressed as product of several functions in some ''H<sup>q</sup>'', ''q''&nbsp;>&nbsp;1.

==Martingale ''H<sup>p</sup>''==
Let (''M<sub>n</sub>'')<sub>''n''≥0</sub> be a [[Martingale (probability theory)|martingale]] on some probability space (Ω,&nbsp;Σ,&nbsp;''P''), with respect to an increasing sequence of σ-fields (Σ<sub>''n''</sub>)<sub>''n''≥0</sub>. Assume for simplicity that Σ is equal to the σ-field generated by the sequence (Σ<sub>''n''</sub>)<sub>''n''≥0</sub>. The ''maximal function'' of the martingale is defined by

:<math> M^* = \sup_{n \ge 0} \, |M_n|.</math>

Let 1 ≤ ''p'' < ∞. The martingale (''M<sub>n</sub>'')<sub>''n''≥0</sub> belongs to ''martingale''-''H<sup>p</sup>'' when ''M*'' ∈ ''L<sup>p</sup>''.

If ''M*'' ∈ ''L<sup>p</sup>'', the martingale (''M<sub>n</sub>'')<sub>''n''≥0</sub> is bounded in ''L<sup>p</sup>''; hence it converges almost surely to some function ''f'' by the [[Doob's martingale convergence theorems|martingale convergence theorem]]. Moreover, ''M<sub>n</sub>'' converges to ''f'' in ''L<sup>p</sup>''-norm by the [[dominated convergence theorem]]; hence ''M<sub>n</sub>'' can be expressed as conditional expectation of ''f'' on Σ<sub>''n''</sub>. It is thus possible to identify martingale-''H<sup>p</sup>'' with the subspace of ''L<sup>p</sup>''(Ω,&nbsp;Σ,&nbsp;''P'') consisting of those ''f'' such that the martingale

:<math>M_n = \operatorname E \bigl( f | \Sigma_n \bigr)</math>

belongs to martingale-''H<sup>p</sup>''.

[[Doob's martingale inequality|Doob's maximal inequality]] implies that martingale-''H<sup>p</sup>'' coincides with ''L<sup>p</sup>''(Ω,&nbsp;Σ,&nbsp;''P'') when 1 < ''p'' < ∞.  The interesting space is martingale-''H''<sup>1</sup>, whose dual is martingale-BMO {{harv|Garsia|1973}}.

The Burkholder–Gundy inequalities (when ''p''&nbsp;>&nbsp;1) and the Burgess Davis inequality (when ''p'' = 1) relate the ''L<sup>p</sup>''-norm of the maximal function to that of the ''square function'' of the martingale

:<math> S(f) = \left( |M_0|^2 + \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |M_{n+1} - M_n|^2 \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}. </math>

Martingale-''H<sup>p</sup>'' can be defined by saying that ''S''(''f'')∈ ''L<sup>p</sup>'' {{harv|Garsia|1973}}.

Martingales with continuous time parameter can also be considered. A direct link with the classical theory is obtained via the complex [[Wiener process|Brownian motion]] (''B<sub>t</sub>'') in the complex plane, starting from the point ''z'' = 0 at time ''t'' = 0. Let τ denote the hitting time of the unit circle. For every holomorphic function ''F'' in the unit disk,

:<math> M_t = F(B_{t \wedge \tau}) </math>

is a martingale, that belongs to martingale-''H<sup>p</sup>'' iff ''F''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''H<sup>p</sup>'' {{Harv |Burkholder|Gundy|Silverstein|1971}}.

=== Example===
In this example, Ω = [0, 1] and Σ<sub>''n''</sub> is the finite field generated by the [[Dyadic_cubes|dyadic]] partition of [0, 1] into 2<sup>''n''</sup> intervals of length 2<sup>−''n''</sup>,  for every ''n'' ≥ 0. If a function ''f'' on [0, 1] is represented by its expansion on the [[Haar wavelet|Haar system]] (''h<sub>k</sub>'')

:<math> f = \sum c_k h_k,</math>

then the martingale-''H''<sup>1</sup> norm of ''f'' can be defined by the ''L''<sup>1</sup> norm of the square function

:<math> \int_0^1 \Bigl( \sum |c_k h_k(x)|^2 \Bigr)^{\frac{1}{2}} \, \mathrm{d}x.</math>

This space, sometimes denoted by ''H''<sup>1</sup>(δ), is isomorphic to the classical real ''H''<sup>1</sup> space on the circle {{harv |Müller|2005}}.  The Haar system is an [[Schauder basis|unconditional basis]] for ''H''<sup>1</sup>(δ).
